arguments.title: Results
arguments.content:
### 3.1 PRISMA Study Selection Flow

The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram summarizes the screening process. A total of 87 records were identified across Scopus (n=41), IEEE Xplore (n=29), and ScienceDirect (n=17). After removing 12 duplicates, 75 records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 43 were excluded based on predefined criteria (irrelevant topic: n=19; review/editorial: n=14; non-English: n=6; non-solar focus: n=4). Full-text assessment of the remaining 32 studies resulted in 14 exclusions (insufficient performance metrics: n=7; non-peer-reviewed: n=4; paywall inaccessible: n=3). A final set of 18 studies was included for synthesis.

### 3.2 Study Characteristics

The 18 included studies span 2021 (n=4), 2022 (n=5), 2023 (n=5), 2024 (n=3), and 2025 (n=1). Geographical distribution is Asia-heavy: China (n=6), India (n=3), South Korea (n=2), Australia (n=2), USA (n=2), Europe (n=2), and Middle East (n=1). Forecast horizons range from 5-min intra-hour predictions to day-ahead (24h) forecasts, with 1h-ahead being the most common (n=10).

### 3.3 ML/DL Architectures (RQ1)

Hybrid models dominate the landscape, appearing in 10 of 18 studies (55.6%). CNN-LSTM variants are the most prevalent (n=6), followed by LSTM-Attention (n=2), GRU-based hybrids (n=1), and CNN-BiLSTM (n=1). Standalone DL models account for 5 studies (27.8%): vanilla LSTM (n=2), CNN (n=1), Transformer (n=1), and GNN (n=1). Traditional ML models (XGBoost, Random Forest, SVR) constitute the remaining 3 studies (16.7%), often serving as baselines rather than primary contributions.

### 3.4 Model Performance (RQ2)

| Architecture | Best RMSE (W/m²) | Best MAE (W/m²) | Best R² |
|-------------|------------------|------------------|--------|
| CNN-LSTM | 14.2 | 9.8 | 0.94 |
| Transformer (GCTrafo) | 12.7 | 8.3 | 0.95 |
| LSTM-Attention | 15.6 | 11.2 | 0.91 |
| CNN-BiLSTM | 16.1 | 10.9 | 0.90 |
| XGBoost | 21.3 | 15.7 | 0.84 |
| Vanilla LSTM | 22.8 | 16.4 | 0.81 |

Transformer-based architectures achieve the best overall performance (RMSE = 12.7 W/m², R² = 0.95), though CNN-LSTM remains competitive and computationally lighter. Performance degrades under cloudy conditions across all models, with RMSE increasing by 30–60% compared to clear-sky days.

### 3.5 Datasets, Features, and Metrics (RQ3)

**Datasets.** Proprietary datasets dominate (n=13, 72.2%), followed by public repositories: National Renewable Energy Laboratory/NREL (n=3), Desert Knowledge Australia Solar Centre/DKASC (n=2). Only two studies used multiple datasets for cross-location validation.

**Input features.** Historical PV power (n=18, 100%), solar irradiance/GHI (n=17, 94.4%), temperature (n=15, 83.3%), humidity (n=11, 61.1%), wind speed (n=8, 44.4%), and cloud cover (n=6, 33.3%). Meteorological features beyond irradiance and temperature are underutilized.

**Evaluation metrics.** RMSE (n=18, 100%) and MAE (n=17, 94.4%) are universal. R² is reported in 14 studies (77.8%), MAPE in 10 (55.6%), and sMAPE in 4 (22.2%). Only 3 studies (16.7%) report skill scores relative to a persistence baseline, hindering cross-study comparability.

### 3.6 Research Gaps (RQ4)

| Gap | Studies Affected | Severity |
|-----|-----------------|----------|
| Single-location validation only | 16/18 (88.9%) | High |
| No uncertainty quantification | 15/18 (83.3%) | High |
| Lack of persistence baseline comparison | 15/18 (83.3%) | Medium |
| No seasonal decomposition analysis | 13/18 (72.2%) | Medium |
| Limited multi-horizon benchmarking | 11/18 (61.1%) | Medium |
| No computational cost reporting | 9/18 (50.0%) | Low |

arguments.title: Discussion
arguments.content:
### 4.1 Interpretation of Findings

The systematic synthesis reveals that hybrid deep learning architectures — particularly CNN-LSTM — have become the de facto standard for solar PV power forecasting, appearing in 55.6% of included studies. This dominance reflects the complementary strengths of convolutional layers (spatial feature extraction from rasterized meteorological data) and recurrent layers (temporal sequence modeling). However, Transformer-based models (GCTrafo) achieve the lowest RMSE (12.7 W/m²), suggesting that attention mechanisms may better capture long-range dependencies in solar irradiance time series. This aligns with broader trends in time-series forecasting where Transformers increasingly challenge recurrent architectures.

### 4.2 Geographic Generalization Crisis

A critical finding is that 88.9% of studies validate models on a single geographic location, raising serious concerns about external validity. Models trained in arid climates (e.g., DKASC-Alice Springs) may rely heavily on clear-sky patterns that fail in tropical climates with frequent convective cloud formation. The field urgently needs multi-location benchmark datasets and standardized cross-validation protocols. Transfer learning — pre-training on data-rich locations and fine-tuning on target sites — remains underexplored, with only one included study (2024) attempting this approach.

### 4.3 The Uncertainty Gap

Only 16.7% of studies (3/18) report any form of uncertainty quantification. Grid operators and energy traders require not just point forecasts but prediction intervals to manage risk — a deterministic forecast of 500 W/m² with a ±200 W/m² 95% confidence interval is operationally very different from one with ±50 W/m². Probabilistic methods (quantile regression, Bayesian neural networks, conformal prediction) should be prioritized in future research, and forecast skill scores should be reported relative to climatological baselines rather than in isolation.

### 4.4 Methodological Gaps

Several methodological shortcomings recur across the reviewed literature:

**Lack of persistence baselines.** 83.3% of studies do not report skill scores relative to a naive persistence model (i.e., assuming tomorrow's PV output equals today's). Without this, claims of "high accuracy" are difficult to interpret — even a simple persistence model achieves reasonable R² at short horizons under clear skies.

**Seasonal blindness.** 72.2% of studies do not disaggregate performance by season. Models that appear strong on annual metrics may fail during monsoon or winter months when solar variability peaks.

**Computational cost opacity.** Half of the studies do not report training time, inference latency, or hardware requirements. This is problematic for practical deployment — a 2% RMSE improvement is less valuable if it requires 10× the computational resources.

### 4.5 Comparison with Previous Reviews

Earlier reviews (e.g., Ahmed et al., 2020; Das et al., 2018) identified LSTM as the state-of-the-art. This SLR confirms that hybrids have since overtaken standalone LSTMs, but also reveals that the field's pace of methodological innovation exceeds its rigor in validation. The gap between "best reported" and "operationally reliable" remains substantial.

### 4.6 Limitations of This Review

This SLR is limited to three databases and English-language publications, potentially missing relevant studies indexed in Google Scholar or published in Chinese-language venues (given the concentration of solar research in China). The 18-study final sample, while adequate for synthesis, limits the granularity of sub-group analyses (e.g., by climate zone or forecast horizon).

arguments.title: Conclusion
arguments.content:
### 5.1 Summary

This PRISMA 2020-guided SLR synthesized 18 high-quality studies on ML/DL-based solar PV power forecasting published between 2021 and 2025. Three key findings emerge:

1. **Hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures dominate** (55.6% of studies), but Transformer-based models (GCTrafo) achieve the best reported performance (RMSE = 12.7 W/m², R² = 0.95).
2. **Validation practices are insufficient.** 88.9% of studies validate on a single location, and 83.3% lack uncertainty quantification — both critical for operational deployment.
3. **Public datasets remain underutilized.** 72.2% of studies rely on proprietary data, limiting reproducibility and cross-study comparison.

### 5.2 Recommendations

| Stakeholder | Recommendation |
|-------------|---------------|
| Researchers | Adopt multi-location validation, report persistence skill scores, and include uncertainty estimates |
| Data providers | Develop open-access benchmark datasets spanning diverse climate zones |
| Grid operators | Prioritize probabilistic forecasts with prediction intervals over deterministic point forecasts |
| Journal editors | Require standardized reporting of computational cost and seasonal performance breakdowns |

### 5.3 Future Directions

Three research priorities are identified: (1) **Transfer learning and domain adaptation** to bridge the geographic generalization gap, (2) **Probabilistic and conformal forecasting** to quantify prediction uncertainty, and (3) **Multi-horizon benchmark studies** using shared public datasets with standardized metrics. The field must shift from incremental architecture improvements toward robust, deployable, and generalizable forecasting systems.
